prompt: What is the Chinchilla-optimal ratio of training tokens to parameters, and which paper established it?
reference: About 20 tokens per parameter. Hoffmann et al. 2022 (DeepMind), 'Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models'. Chinchilla was a 70B model trained on 1.4T tokens.
grading_notes: Accept 20:1 or ~20 tokens/param. Bonus for 70B/1.4T or that Gopher (280B) was undertrained. Mark wrong if ratio is off by >2x or paper misattributed.

prompt: In statistics, what is the term for the situation where the functional form of a fitted model (e.g. a 3-parameter power law) cannot represent the true data-generating process, no matter how the parameters are fit?
reference: Model misspecification (also: specification error).
grading_notes: Accept 'misspecification' or 'specification error'. 'Underfitting' alone is incomplete.

prompt: Does the transformer KV cache grow linearly or quadratically with sequence length? Give the formula for its size in bytes.
reference: Linearly. Size ≈ 2 × L × H_kv × d_head × N × bytes_per_element (2 for keys and values; L layers; H_kv key/value heads; d_head head dim; N tokens). The O(n^2) cost is attention compute, not cache storage.
grading_notes: Must say linear. Formula must include factor 2, layers, heads, head dim, seq len. Accept H instead of H_kv if GQA not mentioned.

prompt: Roughly how many bytes of KV cache per token does Llama-2-70B need in fp16? Show the arithmetic.
reference: ~320 KB/token: 2 × 80 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 head-dim × 2 bytes = 327,680 bytes. (GQA with 8 KV heads.)
grading_notes: Accept 320–328 KB. If model assumes 64 KV heads (no GQA) and gets ~2.5 MB, mark wrong but note the error type.

prompt: In self-attention, what are the distinct roles of queries, keys, and values, and are values derived from Q or K?
reference: Q and K are matched (dot product + softmax) to decide where to attend; V carries the content that gets aggregated by those weights. All three are separate linear projections of the input; V is not derived from Q or K.
grading_notes: Must state V is an independent projection and that QK determine weights, V determines content.

prompt: What is the key idea of FlashAttention, who wrote it, and what year?
reference: IO-aware exact attention: tile Q/K/V so the attention matrix never materializes in HBM, using online softmax and recomputation in the backward pass to trade FLOPs for memory bandwidth. Dao, Fu, Ermon, Rudra, Ré; NeurIPS 2022.
grading_notes: Must mention tiling/not materializing N×N matrix and memory-bandwidth motivation. Tri Dao + 2022 sufficient for attribution.

prompt: Why does softmax attention have far higher associative-memory capacity than linear attention? Relate it to modern Hopfield networks.
reference: Linear readout sums interference from every stored key proportional to similarity, so capacity is ~d_k. Exponential (softmax) weighting suppresses weakly similar keys multiplicatively, acting like a soft nearest-neighbor lookup; capacity grows exponentially in d_k. This is the 'Hopfield Networks is All You Need' (Ramsauer et al., ICLR 2021) / Dense Associative Memory (Krotov & Hopfield, 2016) result.
grading_notes: Needs: linear ~ d capacity, exponential/softmax ~ exp capacity, and connection to modern Hopfield. Attribution to Ramsauer or Krotov&Hopfield is a bonus.

prompt: What is the classical storage capacity of a Hopfield network with N neurons, as a fraction of N?
reference: About 0.138 N (≈0.14 N) patterns for reliable retrieval (Amit, Gutfreund, Sompolinsky).
grading_notes: Accept 0.138N or 0.14N or ~0.15N.

prompt: Describe the standard MoE router in transformers, and explain what Expert Choice routing changes and why it is problematic at batch size 1 inference.
reference: Standard: a linear projection of the token's residual-stream vector, softmax over experts, top-k (usually 1 or 2) per token. Expert Choice (Zhou et al., Google, NeurIPS 2022) flips it: each expert selects its top-k tokens from the batch, giving perfect load balance. At batch size 1 / autoregressive decoding there is only one token to choose from, so experts can't select among tokens; capacity semantics break and there is a train–inference mismatch.
grading_notes: Must have (a) linear router + top-k, (b) experts choose tokens, (c) batch-1 breaks it.

prompt: What is top-1 routing in the Switch Transformer, and who authored that paper?
reference: Each token is sent to exactly one expert (k=1), with a load-balancing auxiliary loss. Fedus, Zoph, Shazeer (Google), 2021/JMLR 2022.
grading_notes: k=1 and Fedus/Zoph/Shazeer.

prompt: In MoE language models, do experts in practice tend to specialize by high-level semantic domain or by low-level token/syntactic patterns?
reference: Empirically mostly by token-level / syntactic or shallow lexical patterns rather than clean semantic domains; the main documented exception is language in multilingual models, where routing aligns with language families. Load-balancing losses push against strong specialization.
grading_notes: Must say token/syntactic-level, not semantic domains. Language exception is a bonus.

prompt: Write the recurrent state update for Mamba-2 (SSD) and for Gated DeltaNet, and state the key difference.
reference: Mamba-2: h_t = a_t · h_{t-1} + B_t x_t^T (scalar decay per head + rank-1 additive write; old content only fades). Gated DeltaNet: S_t = α_t · S_{t-1}(I − β_t k_t k_t^T) + β_t v_t k_t^T (gated decay + delta-rule erase-then-write at key k_t). Difference: GDN actively overwrites what was stored at a key, which is why it does better on associative recall.
grading_notes: Accept equivalent notation. Must capture rank-1 additive vs delta-rule erase. Minor index/sign variations OK.

prompt: Who wrote the original Mamba paper and when? What does 'SSD' stand for in Mamba-2?
reference: Albert Gu and Tri Dao, December 2023 (COLM 2024). Mamba-2 (Dao & Gu, ICML 2024, 'Transformers are SSMs'): SSD = State Space Duality.
grading_notes: Gu & Dao, late 2023; SSD = State Space Duality.

prompt: Why can recurrent/SSM layers be trained in parallel despite being recurrences? Name the property and the two main algorithmic approaches.
reference: The per-step state map is affine (linear + decay), so composing maps is associative. Approaches: (1) parallel/Blelloch scan (Mamba-1), (2) chunkwise algorithms that do intra-chunk masked matmuls plus a sequential pass over chunk boundary states (Mamba-2 SSD, GLA/DeltaNet WY representation). Nonlinear RNNs like LSTMs lose associativity.
grading_notes: Must name associativity and at least one of scan / chunked.

prompt: Who is the primary author of RWKV, and what is 'state tuning' in the RWKV community?
reference: Bo Peng (BlinkDL). State tuning: freeze the weights and optimize only the initial recurrent hidden state(s) for a task, used as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning mode.
grading_notes: Bo Peng/BlinkDL required. State tuning = optimize initial state with frozen weights.

prompt: What are GPTQ and AWQ, who proposed them, and what is the core idea of each?
reference: GPTQ (Frantar et al., ICLR 2023): one-shot weight quantization using approximate second-order (OBS/Hessian) error compensation, column by column. AWQ (Lin et al., MIT/Han lab, MLSys 2024 best paper): activation-aware weight quantization — protect ~1% salient weight channels by per-channel scaling chosen from activation statistics.
grading_notes: Both attributions and both core ideas (Hessian-based vs activation-aware scaling).

prompt: If you add zero-mean Gaussian noise of variance σ² to a logit before a sigmoid, what is the probit (MacKay) approximation for the expected output, and what does it imply about effective temperature?
reference: E[σ(z+ε)] ≈ σ(z / sqrt(1 + πσ²/8)). The noise acts like a temperature of sqrt(1 + πσ²/8) > 1, i.e. slight flattening of the expected output.
grading_notes: Formula with πσ²/8 under a square root. Must state flattening/temperature > 1.

prompt: Does weight quantization of an LLM systematically make its output distribution flatter, or is the effect better described as noise? Explain briefly.
reference: First-order it is roughly zero-mean noise in logit space (most tokens barely move, a few flip, concentrated at near-ties and in the low-probability tail). Second-order, because softmax is nonlinear, zero-mean logit noise slightly reduces expected top-token probability (small effective temperature increase). So: mostly noise, with a small systematic flattening.
grading_notes: Accept 'mostly noise with slight flattening'. Mark wrong if claims a large clean temperature change or no systematic effect at all.

prompt: What is GRPO, which paper introduced it, and how does it compute advantages without a value network?
reference: Group Relative Policy Optimization, from DeepSeekMath (Shao et al., 2024). Sample a group of G completions per prompt, compute advantage of each as (reward − group mean) / group std, use PPO-style clipped objective plus KL penalty; no critic.
grading_notes: Must have DeepSeekMath/Shao 2024 and group-mean baseline.

prompt: What does the Brier score measure, give its formula, and is it a proper scoring rule?
reference: Mean squared error between predicted probabilities and binary outcomes: BS = (1/N) Σ (p_i − o_i)². Strictly proper.
grading_notes: Formula and 'strictly proper'.

prompt: How does the Ranked Probability Score relate to the Brier score, and what is its continuous analogue?
reference: RPS is the Brier score applied to cumulative distributions over ordered categories (sum of squared differences between predicted and observed CDFs), equal to the average of K−1 binary Brier scores at each threshold; reduces to Brier when K=2. Continuous analogue: CRPS (equivalently the squared 1-D earth mover's distance).
grading_notes: Must say cumulative/ordinal Brier and CRPS.

prompt: What is the 'pass@k' metric and why does optimizing pass@1 with standard RL tend to reduce sample diversity?
reference: pass@k = probability that at least one of k samples is correct. Standard RL maximizes expected per-sample reward (pass@1), which rewards concentrating mass on the single most reliable solution; this sharpens the policy and causes entropy collapse, hurting pass@k for large k even if pass@1 improves.
grading_notes: Definition plus mode-sharpening/entropy collapse.

prompt: Summarize 'Learning to Compress Prompts with Gist Tokens': authors, venue, mechanism, headline compression.
reference: Jesse Mu, Xiang Lisa Li, Noah Goodman (Stanford), NeurIPS 2023. Instruction-tune the model with a modified attention mask so the prompt can only be attended to through a few inserted 'gist' tokens; the gist tokens' KV activations then stand in for the prompt (zero-shot prefix tuning). Up to ~26× compression, ~40% FLOPs reduction, tested on LLaMA-7B and FLAN-T5-XXL.
grading_notes: Authors/venue + attention-mask mechanism + ~26x.

prompt: What is a 'Cartridge' in the context of LLM long-context serving, and what is the 'self-study' training recipe?
reference: A Cartridge (Eyuboglu et al., Stanford Hazy Research, 2025) is a small trained KV cache representing a corpus, trained offline and loaded at inference instead of putting the corpus in context. Self-study: generate synthetic conversations about the corpus and train the cartridge with a context-distillation objective, since plain next-token prediction on the corpus memorizes but doesn't generalize. Claimed ~38.6× memory reduction and ~26× throughput at ICL-level quality.
grading_notes: Trained KV cache + synthetic QA/context distillation. Numbers are bonus. 27B may not know this (2025).

prompt: Why is prefix tuning provably no more expressive than directly optimizing the initial hidden state for a linear recurrent / SSM model?
reference: The virtual prefix tokens only influence later tokens through the recurrent state they produce; for a linear recurrence any prefix maps to some initial state, so the set of behaviors reachable by prefix tuning is a subset of those reachable by setting the initial state directly.
grading_notes: Must express that prefix only acts via initial state.

prompt: Do sparse autoencoders used in mechanistic interpretability perform dimensionality reduction? Explain.
reference: No — they are typically overcomplete (hidden width many times the residual dimension). The constraint is sparsity (few active features per input), not a bottleneck; the goal is to decompose activations into interpretable, roughly monosemantic features.
grading_notes: Must say overcomplete / not a bottleneck.

prompt: Which 2023 papers popularized sparse autoencoders for decomposing LLM activations into interpretable features?
reference: Anthropic's 'Towards Monosemanticity' (Bricken et al., Oct 2023) and Cunningham et al. 'Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models' (2023).
grading_notes: Either paper suffices; both is full credit.

prompt: What is the group soft-thresholding ('Group ReLU') operator used in group-sparse coding, as a formula?
reference: σ_λ(x_g) = (1 − λ / ||x_g||₂)₊ · x_g, applied per group g; shrinks the whole group toward zero and zeroes it if its ℓ2 norm is below λ.
grading_notes: Formula must have (1 − λ/||x_g||)₊ x_g or equivalent block soft-thresholding.

prompt: What are epistemic neural networks (epinets), who introduced them, and what is the basic architecture?
reference: Osband et al. (DeepMind, 2021; NeurIPS 2023). A small network (the epinet) takes the base network's features plus a random 'epistemic index' z and adds a perturbation to the output; variation across z expresses epistemic uncertainty, giving ensemble-like joint predictions at far lower cost. Includes a fixed random 'prior' network component.
grading_notes: Osband/DeepMind + epistemic index + cheap ensemble substitute.

prompt: What did McGrath et al. (2022) show about AlphaZero's chess knowledge, and what method did they use?
reference: 'Acquisition of Chess Knowledge in AlphaZero' (PNAS 2022, DeepMind with Vladimir Kramnik). Used linear concept probes on internal activations to show human chess concepts (material, mobility, king safety, etc.) emerge in the network during self-play training, and tracked when during training they appear.
grading_notes: Linear probes for human concepts; emergence over training.

prompt: How many input planes does Leela Chess Zero's network take, and how many entries are in its policy head output?
reference: 112 input planes (8×8×112, including 8 steps of history); policy output of 1858 possible moves.

prompt: What does 'computing in an awkward basis on a GPU' mean? Give two examples and how they are fixed.
reference: A computation whose natural mathematical structure doesn't match GPU-friendly patterns (coalesced memory access, warp-aligned work, matmul tiles in multiples of 16/32/64/128). Examples: attention — fixed by FlashAttention's tiling/recomputation; MoE — irregular token-to-expert assignment fixed by permuting/grouping tokens into dense per-expert matmuls. Also non-power-of-2 dims, irregular gather/scatter, reductions along non-contiguous axes.
grading_notes: Concept + two reasonable examples with fixes.

prompt: Why can't you truncate or slice a cached Mamba/linear-attention state at an arbitrary token position the way you can with a transformer KV cache, and how do inference engines handle prefix caching for such models?
reference: The state update (decay and, for delta-rule models, erase) is lossy and not practically invertible, so you can't recover an earlier state from a later one. Engines (vLLM, SGLang) snapshot the fixed-size state at chunk/block boundaries aligned to the chunked-scan kernel, and restore from the nearest snapshot.
grading_notes: Non-invertibility + checkpoint at block boundaries.

prompt: What was the central experimental result of the 2024 'Accuracy is Not All You Need' paper on LLM quantization?
reference: Dutta et al. (Microsoft, 2024): compressed/quantized models can match the baseline on benchmark accuracy while a substantial fraction of individual answers flip (correct↔incorrect) — 'flips' — so accuracy hides large per-sample divergence; they propose KL divergence and flip rate as better metrics.
grading_notes: Flips / accuracy hides divergence; KL as a metric.

prompt: Explain the NBA team-foul penalty ('bonus') rules, including the last-two-minutes rule and overtime.
reference: A team is in the penalty when the opponent commits its 5th team foul in a quarter; from then on, non-shooting defensive fouls give two free throws. In the last two minutes of a period, the 2nd team foul in that window also puts the team in the penalty if not already there. Team fouls reset each quarter. In overtime the penalty starts on the 4th team foul.
grading_notes: 5th foul, 2-in-last-2-minutes, 4th in OT. Offensive fouls don't count toward penalty (bonus).

prompt: Who leads the NBA in the product of championships won as a player times championships won as a head coach? Give the numbers.
reference: It's a tie at 22: Phil Jackson (2 as a Knicks player: 1970, 1973; 11 as a coach: 6 Bulls, 5 Lakers → 2×11=22) and Bill Russell (11 as a Celtics player; 2 as player-coach in 1968 and 1969 → 11×2=22).
grading_notes: Full credit: both at 22. Partial: names Jackson or Russell with correct individual numbers. Wrong: Jackson with 11 as player or 13 as coach (a common hallucination), or Russell with 0 as coach.

prompt: Describe Kyrie Irving's most famous clutch shot: the game, the opponent, the time remaining, and the final score.
reference: Game 7 of the 2016 NBA Finals, Cavaliers vs. Warriors. A step-back three over Stephen Curry with ~53 seconds left to break an 89–89 tie; Cavs won 93–89, Cleveland's first NBA title and first championship comeback from 3–1 down in the Finals.
grading_notes: 2016 Finals G7, three over Curry, 93-89. Time ~53s (accept 'under a minute').

prompt: In which seasons was Jimmy Butler named to an NBA All-Defensive team, and which team? Also, does his nickname 'Jimmy Buckets' refer to his defense?
reference: All-Defensive Second Team five times: 2014, 2015, 2016, 2018, 2021 (never First Team). 'Jimmy Buckets' refers to his scoring, not defense.
grading_notes: Accept 4 or 5 selections if years are correct; must be Second Team only; must say the nickname is about scoring.

prompt: How do NBA rookie scale contracts work for first-round picks (length, options, salary range relative to scale)?
reference: First-round picks sign scale contracts set by draft slot: two guaranteed years plus team options for years 3 and 4; teams may pay 80–120% of the scale amount (almost always 120%). Second-round picks and undrafted players are not on the scale.
grading_notes: 2+2 structure, 80–120%, first round only.

prompt: What does the Defect's card 'Scrape' do in Slay the Spire, and which archetype is it built for?
reference: 1-cost Skill: draw 4 cards (5 when upgraded), then discard all drawn cards that don't cost 0. Built for the 0-cost 'Claw' archetype (Claw, All for One, Beam Cell, etc.).
grading_notes: Draw 4/5, discard non-0-cost, Claw/0-cost deck.

prompt: Who developed Slay the Spire, and when did it leave early access? What are the four orb types in the Defect's kit?
reference: Mega Crit (Casey Yano & Anthony Giovannetti); Early Access Nov 2017, full release January 2019. Orbs: Lightning, Frost, Dark, Plasma.
grading_notes: Mega Crit, 2019 full release, four orbs.

prompt: Describe how Chrono Ark differs from Slay the Spire in party structure and enemy timing.
reference: Chrono Ark is a party-based roguelike deckbuilder: you field four characters from a roster (~20), each contributing their own skill cards to one shared deck; the protagonist Lucy supports rather than fights directly. Enemy actions are triggered by the number of cards you play (a countdown) rather than only turn boundaries, so sequencing and 'Swiftness' (cards that don't advance timers) matter. Healing, overheal, and 'death's door' are central; developed by Korean studio Al Fine, 1.0 in 2024.
grading_notes: Shared party deck + card-count-based enemy timing are required; Lucy/Al Fine are bonus.
